title: Build a recall, check, and revisit routine
concepts: Familiarity is not the same as recall. After an initial explanation, try reconstructing an idea without looking; the attempt reveals gaps that smooth rereading can hide.
Pair retrieval with feedback. Check your attempt, explain the difference, and try again later rather than rehearsing an unchecked mistake.

Spread encounters across separate sessions. Make the next interval manageable: revisit a shaky idea sooner and a reliably recalled one later, rather than treating one schedule as a rule for every learner.
Once basic procedures make sense, mix related problem types so you must choose an approach. Interleaving is purposeful comparison, not rapidly switching between unrelated distractions.

example.title: Learn to choose between two loop patterns
example.explanation: This worked study plan uses a distinction rather than a memorized answer. A fixed number of repetitions and input that ends at a special value require different stopping decisions. If you cannot yet explain either pattern, begin with a small worked example; independent attempts become more useful once there is something to retrieve. The check is whether you can explain a new case after a gap, not whether the notes look familiar.
steps: Read one example of repeating a known number of times and one example of repeating until a stop value appears.
Close the examples and explain how each pattern decides when to stop. Write a tiny trace from memory.
Compare with the examples. Record one specific correction, such as checking the stop value before adding it to a total.
In a later session, classify a mixed pair of new situations before writing any code; explain why you chose each stopping rule.
Schedule another short check. If you needed a hint, shorten the gap or simplify the next prompt instead of only rereading for longer.

title: Make focused work sustainable
concepts: Give a session one observable goal, such as explaining a concept or checking a trace. A smaller finish line makes it easier to notice progress than a vague instruction to study everything.

Protect attention before starting: silence nonessential notifications, clear unrelated tabs, and keep a place to note tasks for later. A written reminder lets an interruption wait without requiring an immediate switch.
A work-and-break timer is a planning aid, not a test of endurance. The familiar Pomodoro pattern uses 25 minutes of work and 5 minutes of rest, but adjust the interval to the task and your needs.

Notice fatigue rather than treating every error as lack of effort. Repeated rereading or escalating mistakes can signal a need for rest. Regular sleep supports learning and attention; it does not replace practice or guarantee an anxiety-free exam.

example.title: Reset a study block that has stopped working
example.explanation: Suppose you have spent several minutes rereading one explanation and cannot summarize it. The aim is to change the conditions, not punish yourself with a longer session. A break and a smaller retrieval task provide information about what you need next. This is a flexible routine, not a promise that a timer will remove every distraction or difficulty.
steps: Pause and write a restart cue: Explain why this loop terminates in two sentences.
Take a short break away from the material; stretch, move, or get water if useful.
Return with only the relevant example open and choose a manageable work interval.
Attempt the two-sentence explanation before reopening the solution. If a concept is missing, study that specific prerequisite.
Stop at your planned finish time and note the next task, preserving time for your usual sleep routine.

title: Turn a practice exam into a targeted plan
concepts: A practice paper measures more than topic knowledge: it also reveals pacing, interpretation, and checking habits. Use the permitted resources and timing of the real assessment when rehearsing those conditions.
Budget time in proportion to marks while reserving a checking period. If progress stalls, record useful working, mark the question, and move on when the assessment format permits returning later.
Classify mistakes by cause as well as topic. A missing concept, a misread instruction, an arithmetic slip, and unfinished work need different follow-up actions.

Review is complete only when it changes the next attempt. Re-solve a similar problem without the solution after a gap; copying the mark scheme demonstrates transcription, not independent understanding.
Reduce avoidable uncertainty before exam day: check the location, time, permitted materials, and relevant rules. Keep final revision manageable instead of sacrificing rest to a large new topic.

example.title: Review a short mock without chasing only the score
example.explanation: Imagine a 40-minute practice with three lost marks from a loop boundary, two from missing a multi-select instruction, and an unfinished final question. Those outcomes suggest three separate interventions. Learning the loop rule will not by itself fix instruction reading or pacing. The plan below produces a specific next action for each cause, then checks whether the action helped.
steps: Attempt the practice before opening its solutions. Note where time ran out and which answers were uncertain.
Trace the loop boundary using the first and last accepted values; then solve a new boundary example without looking.
Add a brief instruction check before answering: how many selections or pieces of working are requested?
For another 40-minute practice, reserve four minutes for checking and divide the remaining 36 minutes by the paper's mark allocation.
After a gap, try a comparable practice and review the same three causes. Update the plan from the evidence, not just the total score.
